questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
questions.challenge_mechanism: The single-layer greenhouse model predicts a surface temperature of 303 K where the measured value is 288 K, so the item hands the candidate a model that demonstrably over-predicts and then asks them to find the leak. Inverting the balance for the fraction of longwave radiation that escapes directly gives about 22%, which is the atmospheric window, and no candidate can reach it without setting up the balance themselves.
questions.question: The solar constant at the Earth's orbit is $S = 1361\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, the planetary albedo is $\alpha = 0.30$, and the Stefan–Boltzmann constant is $\sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-4}}$. The measured mean surface temperature of the Earth is $288\ \mathrm{K}$. Treat the Earth as a sphere in a steady state, so that the mean power absorbed equals the mean power radiated to space.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the mean power absorbed per unit area of the Earth's surface, averaged over the whole sphere, is $\dfrac{S(1-\alpha)}{4}$, and calculate its value. Explain in one sentence why the factor of four appears.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence determine the effective radiating temperature of the Earth, that is, the temperature of a black body that would radiate that power per unit area to space.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A simple model treats the atmosphere as a single layer that is transparent to solar radiation and completely opaque to infrared. In this model the atmosphere absorbs all the surface's infrared emission and re-radiates equally upwards and downwards. Show that this leads to a surface temperature of $2^{1/4}$ times the effective temperature, calculate that temperature, and state by how much it exceeds the measured value.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suppose instead that a fraction $f$ of the surface's infrared emission escapes directly to space through the atmospheric window, and that the remaining fraction is absorbed by the atmosphere and re-radiated equally up and down. Determine the value of $f$ for which the balance gives the measured surface temperature of $288\ \mathrm{K}$, and evaluate whether the single-layer model in part (c) is a fair description of the real atmosphere.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The Earth intercepts solar radiation over its cross-sectional area $\pi R^{2}$, so the power intercepted is $S\pi R^{2}$ and the fraction absorbed is $(1-\alpha)$ of that. **(M1)** This is spread over the whole surface area $4\pi R^{2}$, so the mean absorbed power per unit area is **(M1)**
$$\frac{S(1-\alpha)\pi R^{2}}{4\pi R^{2}} = \frac{S(1-\alpha)}{4} = \frac{1361 \times 0.70}{4} = 238\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$$ **(A1)**
The factor of four appears because a sphere presents a disc of area $\pi R^{2}$ to a parallel beam but radiates, and here absorbs on average, over an area four times as large. **(A1)**

**(b)** In steady state the mean emitted power per unit area equals the absorbed value, so $\sigma T_{e}^{4} = 238$. **(M1)**
$$T_{e} = \left(\frac{238}{5.67 \times 10^{-8}}\right)^{1/4} = (4.20 \times 10^{9})^{1/4} = 255\ \mathrm{K}$$ **(A1)(A1)**
which is about $-18\ \mathrm{^{\circ}C}$. **(A1)** This is the temperature the Earth would have with no greenhouse effect at all, and it is well below the freezing point of water.

**(c)** Let the surface emit $\sigma T_{s}^{4}$. The atmosphere absorbs all of it and re-radiates $\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma T_{s}^{4}$ upwards and the same downwards. **(M1)** The balance at the top of the atmosphere is therefore
$$\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma T_{s}^{4} = 238 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \sigma T_{s}^{4} = 476$$
while $\sigma T_{e}^{4} = 238$, so $\sigma T_{s}^{4} = 2\,\sigma T_{e}^{4}$ and **(M1)**
$$T_{s} = 2^{1/4}\,T_{e} = 1.189 \times 255 = 303\ \mathrm{K}$$ **(A1)**
This exceeds the measured $288\ \mathrm{K}$ by about $15\ \mathrm{K}$. **(A1)** The model therefore predicts a stronger greenhouse effect than the Earth actually has.

**(d)** The surface emits $\sigma T_{s}^{4}$ with $T_{s} = 288\ \mathrm{K}$, which is $5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times 288^{4} = 390\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. **(A1)** Of this, $f$ escapes directly and $(1-f)$ is absorbed by the atmosphere, which re-radiates half of that upwards. The total escaping to space is therefore **(M1)**
$$f\,\sigma T_{s}^{4} + \frac{(1-f)}{2}\,\sigma T_{s}^{4} = \sigma T_{s}^{4}\,\frac{(1+f)}{2}$$
Setting this equal to the absorbed $238\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$: **(M1)**
$$\frac{(1+f)}{2} = \frac{238}{390} = 0.611 \quad\Rightarrow\quad f = 2(0.611) - 1 = 0.22$$
So about $22\%$ of the surface's infrared emission escapes directly to space. **(A1)** The single-layer model of part (c) is therefore not a fair description: it assumes the atmosphere is completely opaque to infrared, which would set $f = 0$ and give $303\ \mathrm{K}$, whereas the real atmosphere is partially transparent in the infrared and the direct escape is roughly a fifth of the surface emission. The model is still useful, because it produces the right order for the greenhouse warming and it identifies the mechanism — absorption and re-radiation rather than reflection — but it over-predicts the magnitude because it ignores the window and because it treats the atmosphere as a single isothermal layer when in reality it radiates to space from a range of altitudes.
questions.markscheme_notes: (a) Award (M1) for the intercepted area $\pi R^{2}$ and (M1) for dividing by the surface area $4\pi R^{2}$; the verbal mark is for saying that the beam is intercepted by a disc while the average is taken over a sphere, and 'the Sun only shines on one side' is not sufficient on its own. (b) Accept $254$ to $256\ \mathrm{K}$. A candidate who forgets the factor of four in part (a) gets $360\ \mathrm{K}$ here and should be given follow-through only if the error is consistent. (c) The mark is for the factor of two in the balance; accept $302$ to $304\ \mathrm{K}$. A candidate who writes $T_{s} = 2T_{e}$ has used a factor of sixteen in the emission rather than two, and should lose the temperature mark but can still earn the comparison on follow-through. (d) Accept $f$ from $0.20$ to $0.24$. The evaluation must name the window or the partial transparency of the atmosphere; a candidate who says only that the model is wrong has not said why, and the remark about the isothermal layer is the strongest available point but is not required.
questions.explanation:
This question is arranged so that a model a student can build turns out to be wrong in an informative way, and the size of the error tells them something about the atmosphere. Part (b) gives $255\ \mathrm{K}$, which is a genuinely startling number the first time it appears: with no greenhouse effect at all the Earth sits eighteen degrees below the freezing point of water, and the habitability of the planet is entirely a consequence of the infrared opacity of its atmosphere. That single comparison is worth more than any amount of description.

Part (c) then makes the simplest possible greenhouse model and it overshoots. The single fully-opaque layer re-radiates half of what it absorbs downwards, so the surface has to emit twice what escapes to space, and the fourth root turns that factor of two into only $18\%$ on the temperature: $303\ \mathrm{K}$ against the measured $288\ \mathrm{K}$. The model is not useless — it gets the magnitude of the greenhouse warming roughly right and it shows that the mechanism is re-radiation rather than trapping, which is the misconception the word 'greenhouse' invites. But it is $15\ \mathrm{K}$ too warm, and part (d) asks where the extra heat got to.

The answer is the atmospheric window. Setting up the balance with a fraction $f$ escaping directly is a small piece of algebra that most candidates can do once they see it, and it produces $f \approx 0.22$. That number has a physical meaning: roughly a fifth of the surface's infrared emission leaves the planet without ever being absorbed, in the wavelength range between about $8$ and $13\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ where water vapour and carbon dioxide are comparatively transparent. It is also the reason the model in part (c) fails, and it is the reason adding carbon dioxide warms the surface at all: the gas narrows the window. A student who has derived $f$ themselves is in a much better position to understand that than one who has been told it.

provenance.adaptation: Original item built on the standard planetary energy-balance model. The measured surface temperature of 288 K and the solar constant of 1361 W/m2 are given, and the four-part structure — absorbed flux, effective temperature, single-layer over-prediction, then inversion for the window fraction — was constructed so that the last part has a determinate answer the candidate must reach rather than a value to be quoted. All four numbers were recomputed in Python.

verification.method: The absorbed flux, the effective temperature, the single-layer surface temperature and the inverted window fraction were all recomputed in Python to full precision, and the final balance was checked by substituting the recovered value of f back into the expression for the power escaping to space.
solution_skeleton: average the intercepted solar power over the whole spherical surface to obtain the absorbed flux
invert the Stefan-Boltzmann law to convert a flux into an effective radiating temperature
write the top-of-atmosphere balance for a single opaque layer and take the fourth root of the resulting factor of two
allow a fraction of the surface emission to escape directly and solve the balance for that fraction at the measured temperature
judge the model by the size and direction of its error rather than by whether it is exactly right

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Apply the single-layer atmosphere model as given, obtain a surface temperature, and report it as the predicted value.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The single-layer model over-predicts the surface temperature by about fifteen kelvin against the measured value, so the model has to be treated as a design to be diagnosed rather than as a calculation to be completed.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: A surface temperature of about three hundred and three kelvin reported without comment, and no fraction of directly escaping longwave radiation extracted from the measured value.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.challenge_mechanism: The velocity selector is a standard piece of apparatus and the trap is that its output speed is fixed by the fields and not by the source, so every ion that emerges has the same speed whatever its mass. Everything downstream then depends on that one fact, and the final part asks whether two isotopes 3 u apart are actually separable, which the radius ratio of 1.013 answers in a way that a qualitative discussion cannot.
questions.question: A mass spectrometer uses a velocity selector followed by a deflecting chamber. In the selector, a uniform electric field of strength $E = 8.0 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ and a uniform magnetic field of flux density $B = 0.40\ \mathrm{T}$ are at right angles to each other and to the beam, arranged so that the electric and magnetic forces on a positive ion oppose. Ions that pass through the selector without deflection enter a second chamber containing only a uniform magnetic field of flux density $B' = 0.80\ \mathrm{T}$ perpendicular to their velocity. Take $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$ and the unified atomic mass unit as $1.66 \times 10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that an ion passes through the selector undeflected only if its speed is $v = E/B$, and calculate that speed. State, with a reason, whether this speed depends on the mass or the charge of the ion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In the second chamber an ion describes a semicircular path and strikes a detector. Show that the distance between the entry point and the point of impact is $d = \dfrac{2mv}{qB'}$, and calculate this distance for a singly ionised ion of uranium-238.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The beam also contains singly ionised uranium-235. Determine the separation of the two impact points on the detector, and determine the ratio of the two path radii.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate whether this instrument can be used to separate the two isotopes in practice, referring to your answer to (c) and to one further feature of the apparatus that the calculation does not include.

questions.answer:
**(a)** For an undeflected path the net force is zero, so the electric and magnetic forces are equal in magnitude: **(M1)**
$$qE = Bqv \quad\Rightarrow\quad v = \frac{E}{B} = \frac{8.0 \times 10^{4}}{0.40} = 2.0 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$ **(A1)(A1)**
The speed does not depend on the mass or on the magnitude of the charge, because $q$ cancels in $qE = Bqv$; it depends only on the two field strengths. **(A1)** Doubling the charge doubles both forces and leaves the balance untouched. The selector therefore transmits ions of one speed and rejects all others, whatever their mass.

**(b)** In the second chamber the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it provides the centripetal force and the path is an arc of a circle: **(M1)**
$$B'qv = \frac{mv^{2}}{r} \quad\Rightarrow\quad r = \frac{mv}{qB'}$$
The ion travels a semicircle, so the distance from entry to impact is the diameter $d = 2r$: **(M1)**
$$d = \frac{2mv}{qB'} = \frac{2 \times 238 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \times 2.0 \times 10^{5}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 0.80}$$
$$d = \frac{1.58 \times 10^{-19}}{1.28 \times 10^{-19}} = 1.23\ \mathrm{m}$$ **(A1)(A1)**

**(c)** The mass of a uranium-235 ion is $\dfrac{235}{238}$ of the uranium-238 mass, and since $r \propto m$ at fixed $v$, $q$ and $B'$, the radii scale in the same ratio. **(M1)** For uranium-238, $r = d/2 = 0.617\ \mathrm{m}$, so for uranium-235 **(M1)**
$$r_{235} = 0.617 \times \frac{235}{238} = 0.610\ \mathrm{m}$$
The impact points are separated by twice the difference in radii: **(A1)**
$$\Delta = 2(0.6173 - 0.6095) = 1.6 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m} = 16\ \mathrm{mm}$$
and the ratio of the radii is $\dfrac{238}{235} = 1.013$. **(A1)**

**(d)** A separation of $16\ \mathrm{mm}$ on a path about $1.2\ \mathrm{m}$ long is measurable, so in principle the two isotopes can be distinguished. **(A1)** The ratio of $1.013$ is the more telling number: the two radii differ by only about $1.3\%$, so the apparatus has very little margin, and anything that blurs the impact point by more than a few millimetres destroys the separation. **(A1)** One feature the calculation ignores is that the beam entering the selector is not monoenergetic — the ion source produces a spread of speeds, and even the transmitted ions have a small spread because the selector has a finite width and the cancellation is never perfect for ions slightly off the axis. This thermal spread alone typically broadens each impact point by more than $16\ \mathrm{mm}$ unless the ions are first accelerated through a well-defined potential difference, which is why real instruments do so. **(A1)** A second consideration is that a practical separator must also produce useful quantities: the beam current that can be pushed through a $16\ \mathrm{mm}$ slit is small, so separating macroscopic amounts of uranium-235 this way would be extremely slow, which is precisely why isotope separation for fuel is done by other means. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: (a) Award (M1) for equating the two forces and (A1) for the speed; the final mark is for stating that the speed is independent of mass and charge *with the reason that q cancels*, and 'it depends only on the fields' without the cancellation is not enough. (b) Accept $1.22$ to $1.24\ \mathrm{m}$. Candidates who use the diameter and candidates who use the radius should be distinguished: the question asks for the distance from entry to impact, so a candidate who computes $0.617\ \mathrm{m}$ has found the radius and should lose one mark even though the physics is right. (c) Accept $15$ to $17\ \mathrm{mm}$ and a ratio of $1.01$. The scaling argument $r \propto m$ is worth more than recomputing from scratch, and should be credited even if the arithmetic slips. (d) Credit must be given for engaging with the $16\ \mathrm{mm}$ figure rather than asserting that the separation is small; the strongest additional point is the spread of speeds in the beam, and the strongest objection of all is throughput. Do not accept 'friction' or 'air resistance' — the chamber is evacuated.
questions.explanation:
The velocity selector is the conceptual heart of this item, and it is worth being clear about why. Two fields act on the same ion and their forces oppose, and the balance condition $qE = Bqv$ does not contain $q$ or $m$ at all. Every ion that emerges from the selector is therefore travelling at exactly the same speed, $2.0 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, regardless of what it is. Students find this surprising because they expect a mass spectrometer to select by mass, and it does not: the selector fixes the speed, and the deflection chamber then converts mass into radius precisely *because* the speed is already known. Without the selector, $r = mv/qB'$ has two unknowns and nothing can be inferred.

Part (c) is where the item earns its marks. The two uranium isotopes differ by three atomic mass units, which sounds like a great deal, and the resulting radii differ by a factor of $238/235 = 1.013$, which is very little. The detector separation is $16\ \mathrm{mm}$ on a $1.2\ \mathrm{m}$ path. Both of those numbers are needed to evaluate the instrument, and they pull in different directions: $16\ \mathrm{mm}$ is comfortably measurable, and $1.3\%$ is uncomfortably tight. Holding the two together is the actual judgement.

Part (d) asks what the calculation leaves out, and the honest answer is the spread of speeds in the beam. The entire derivation assumes every ion moves at exactly $v = E/B$, and a real ion source produces a distribution. Because the separation is only $1.3\%$ in radius, a spread of more than about half a per cent in speed washes it out completely, which is why real instruments accelerate the ions through a fixed potential difference before they enter. That is a genuine engineering point that follows directly from the numbers the candidate has just computed, and it is a better lesson than any amount of description of how a mass spectrometer works.

provenance.adaptation: Original item. The field strengths were chosen so that the selected speed is a round 2.0 x 10^5 m/s and the uranium-238 diameter is a little over a metre, and the isotope pair 235/238 was chosen because the 3 u difference is historically the case that matters and yet gives a radius ratio of only 1.013. Every figure, including the 16 mm separation, was recomputed in Python.

verification.method: The selected speed, both radii, the impact separation and the radius ratio were recomputed in Python to full precision from m = A * 1.6605e-27 kg, and the limiting speed spread implied by the 1.3% radius difference was checked against the separation.
solution_skeleton: equate the electric and magnetic forces in the crossed fields to eliminate the charge and obtain the selected speed
equate the magnetic force to the centripetal force to express the path radius in terms of mass, speed, charge and field
scale the radius with the mass ratio to obtain the second radius and hence the detector separation
compare the separation with the path size and judge whether the margin is adequate against a realistic beam spread

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Assume that heavier ions leave the selector more slowly and separate the isotopes on the basis of the different speeds they carry out of it.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The selector passes only those ions whose speed equals the ratio of the fields, so every ion that emerges has the same speed whatever its mass; the separation downstream depends on that fixed speed together with the mass, not on any spread of speeds.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: A speed that varies with the ion mass, and a separation of the two isotopes predicted from a difference in speed rather than from the difference in radius at a common speed.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
questions.challenge_mechanism: The arithmetic produces two numbers that nobody believes the first time: a 3 GW reactor consumes 3.2 kg of uranium-235 per day, and the same energy from coal is 8600 tonnes per day. The candidate has to derive both from the same energy per fission, which keeps the comparison honest, and then explain why the fuel cannot simply be a lump of uranium, which requires neutron economy rather than arithmetic.
questions.question: Each fission of a uranium-235 nucleus releases about $200\ \mathrm{MeV}$ of energy and, on average, $2.4$ neutrons. A power station produces $1.0\ \mathrm{GW}$ of electrical power at an overall efficiency of $33\%$. Take $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, the unified atomic mass unit as $1.66 \times 10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$, and the energy density of coal as $30\ \mathrm{MJ\,kg^{-1}}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released by a single fission in joules, and hence the number of fissions taking place each second in the reactor core.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence determine the mass of uranium-235 consumed in the core in one day, and the mass of coal that would have to be burned in one day to produce the same output.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Only about $0.7\%$ of natural uranium is the fissile isotope uranium-235. Determine the mass of natural uranium that must be mined each day to supply the core, assuming the enrichment process extracts all of the uranium-235 and discards the rest.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the uranium in a reactor cannot simply be assembled as a single lump of fissionable material, referring to the average number of neutrons released per fission and to what happens to those neutrons. Your answer should make clear why a moderator is needed in a thermal reactor.

questions.answer:
**(a)** One fission releases **(M1)**
$$200\ \mathrm{MeV} = 200 \times 10^{6} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J} = 3.20 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{J}$$
**(A1)** The electrical output is $1.0\ \mathrm{GW}$, so at $33\%$ efficiency the thermal power of the core is **(M1)**
$$P_{\text{th}} = \frac{1.0 \times 10^{9}}{0.33} = 3.0 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{W}$$
and the number of fissions per second is **(A1)**
$$N = \frac{3.0 \times 10^{9}}{3.20 \times 10^{-11}} = 9.4 \times 10^{19}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$$

**(b)** Each fission consumes one uranium-235 nucleus of mass $235 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27} = 3.90 \times 10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg}$. **(M1)** In one day the number of fissions is $9.4 \times 10^{19} \times 86\,400 = 8.1 \times 10^{24}$, so the mass consumed is **(M1)**
$$m = 8.1 \times 10^{24} \times 3.90 \times 10^{-25} = 3.2\ \mathrm{kg}$$
**(A1)** The energy delivered in one day is $3.0 \times 10^{9} \times 86\,400 = 2.6 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{J}$, so the equivalent mass of coal is **(M1)**
$$m_{\text{coal}} = \frac{2.6 \times 10^{14}}{30 \times 10^{6}} = 8.6 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{kg} \approx 8600\ \mathrm{tonnes}$$
**(A1)** The ratio of the two masses is $\dfrac{8.6 \times 10^{6}}{3.2} \approx 2.7 \times 10^{6}$, so kilogram for kilogram the nuclear fuel releases something like three million times as much energy as the coal. This is the number that makes the comparison worth doing: it is far too large to be recovered by any plausible improvement in the efficiency of a coal plant.

**(c)** Natural uranium is $0.7\%$ uranium-235 by mass, so the mass of natural uranium containing $3.2\ \mathrm{kg}$ of the fissile isotope is **(M1)**
$$m_{\text{nat}} = \frac{3.2}{0.007} = 4.6 \times 10^{2}\ \mathrm{kg} \approx 460\ \mathrm{kg}$$
**(A1)(A1)** This assumes complete extraction. In practice the enrichment process leaves some uranium-235 in the discarded tailings, so rather more than $460\ \mathrm{kg}$ must be mined; if the tails assay is $0.2\%$ rather than zero, the requirement rises to about $630\ \mathrm{kg}$ per day. **(A1)**

**(d)** Each fission releases on average $2.4$ neutrons, so a chain reaction is possible in principle: one fission can initiate more than one further fission. **(A1)** It does not happen automatically, for two reasons. First, some neutrons escape through the surface of the material, and the fraction escaping is large when the lump is small because the surface-to-volume ratio is large; below the critical mass, too many neutrons are lost for the reaction to sustain itself. **(A1)** Second, and more importantly, the neutrons emerge from fission moving fast, with energies of the order of $1\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and the fission cross-section of uranium-235 is very small at those energies — a fast neutron is far more likely to be scattered or to be captured without causing fission than to induce one. **(A1)** A moderator, such as water or graphite, surrounds the fuel and slows the neutrons by elastic collisions with light nuclei until they reach thermal energies of a fraction of an electronvolt, at which the fission cross-section is hundreds of times larger and the chain reaction proceeds. **(A1)** Control rods, made of a material that absorbs neutrons strongly, are then used to remove exactly the surplus above the one neutron per fission needed to sustain the reaction, so that on average exactly one neutron from each fission causes another.
questions.markscheme_notes: (a) Accept $3.2 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{J}$ and $9.3$ to $9.5 \times 10^{19}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The efficiency conversion is the point of the part: a candidate who divides $1.0\ \mathrm{GW}$ by the fission energy without correcting for efficiency has answered a different question and should lose the second mark. (b) Accept $3.1$ to $3.3\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $8.5$ to $8.8 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{kg}$. Note that the mass consumed is the mass actually fissioned, not the mass loaded into the core, which is considerably larger. (c) Accept $450$ to $470\ \mathrm{kg}$; the tails comment is a bonus and should be credited if offered, but candidates are not expected to know the term. (d) Four distinct points are available: the possibility of a chain reaction because more than one neutron is released, the escape of neutrons through the surface and the existence of a critical mass, the low fission cross-section for fast neutrons, and the action of the moderator. Candidates who mention the moderator but not the cross-section have given the mechanism without the reason and should not receive full marks; the word cross-section need not be used, but the idea that fast neutrons do not readily cause fission must be present.
questions.explanation:
The two numbers in part (b) are the reason this item exists. A large power station fissions about three kilograms of uranium a day, and the same output from coal is eight thousand six hundred tonnes. Stated as raw figures they sound like propaganda; derived from $200\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per fission and a chain of unit conversions that the candidate performs themselves, they are simply arithmetic, and the factor of $2.7 \times 10^{6}$ between nuclear and chemical energy density becomes something the student has established rather than been told. Keeping both calculations running from the same fission energy is what makes the comparison trustworthy — there is no separate route to the coal figure that could be quietly adjusted.

Part (c) adds a detail that changes the picture in an interesting direction. Natural uranium is almost entirely uranium-238, which does not fission with thermal neutrons, so the $3.2\ \mathrm{kg}$ actually consumed has to be dug out of about $460\ \mathrm{kg}$ of ore-concentrate per day. That is still small next to eight thousand tonnes of coal, but it is a hundred times larger than the headline figure, and it is the reason enrichment exists as an industry. The assumption that extraction is complete is false and worth flagging, because the discarded material still contains uranium-235 and the tails assay is an economic as much as a physical choice.

Part (d) is the part that cannot be reached by arithmetic, and it is where candidates most often substitute the word 'critical mass' for an explanation. The chain reaction is possible because $2.4 > 1$, but $2.4$ is an average over all neutrons leaving all fissions, and it says nothing about how many of those neutrons go on to cause another fission. Most do not. Some escape through the surface, which is why geometry and size matter and why a critical mass exists at all. More importantly, most of the remainder are moving too fast to be captured efficiently: the fission cross-section of uranium-235 rises by orders of magnitude as the neutron slows, so a reactor without a moderator is not a reactor. That single fact explains why the moderator is there, why the fuel and the moderator have to be interleaved rather than separated, and why a loss of coolant can shut the reaction down rather than run away — a point worth making, since the intuition runs the other way.

provenance.adaptation: Original item. The 200 MeV per fission, the 2.4 neutrons, the 33% efficiency and the 0.7% natural abundance are standard physical data; the four-part chain from fission energy to mining requirement was constructed for this item, and every derived figure including the 630 kg tails-assay case was recomputed in Python.

verification.method: The energy per fission, the thermal power, the fission rate, the daily uranium consumption, the coal equivalent, the natural uranium requirement and the alternative tails-assay case were all recomputed in Python to full precision.
solution_skeleton: convert the energy per fission from electronvolts to joules and divide the thermal power by it to obtain the fission rate
multiply the fission rate by the elapsed time and the mass of one nucleus to obtain the fuel consumed
convert the same delivered energy into a fuel mass using the chemical energy density for comparison
scale the fissile mass by the natural abundance to obtain the mining requirement, and note what complete extraction assumes
account for the fate of the neutrons released per fission, separating surface escape from the low fast-neutron fission cross-section
